passage: Thomas, you want to know why I've stopped coming to anything. Fine. You know the group that sits by the basketball court? On Monday I asked if I could sit with them, and Anushka said, 'Sorry, Noor, it's kind of a closed thing.' A few of them laughed. So that's it. That's how everyone sees me. I'm not someone people want around. Not in this school, not in college, not anywhere. Why would it be different? I've already stopped signing up for the book club and the trek. Why go and get the same answer? You're different, you've known me since we were seven, you have to be nice. Don't make that face. It was one group, I know. But it's the group that counts. Okay, fine, maybe they're not the whole world. It just feels like they are.

qa.q: What did Anushka say when Noor asked to sit with the group?
qa.a: Anushka said, 'Sorry, Noor, it's kind of a closed thing.'

qa.q: Why does one refusal feel like proof about 'anywhere' to Noor?
qa.a: The rejection hurt so much that it feels like a verdict on who Noor is, so one group's answer gets stretched to every school, college and place.

qa.q: What small step could test Noor's conclusion?
qa.a: Noor could go to the book club or the trek anyway and notice how people there actually respond, treating it as a new sample instead of assuming the same answer.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel being told 'you have to be nice'?
qa.a: Thomas may feel brushed aside, since a real friendship is being treated as duty, and sad that Noor is pulling away from everything.

grounding: Shows a teenager refused by one lunch group who concludes no one anywhere will ever accept them and stops signing up for things.

passage: I'm Nitin, Varun's older brother, and I'm only telling what I saw. Varun tried out for the colony's under-15 football group that plays on the big ground every evening. After one session, one of the older boys told him, 'We've got enough players, bro.' That was two weeks ago. Since then Varun has come straight home every day. He deleted the practice-drills app from his phone. When our cousin invited him to join the badminton lot at the community hall, he said, 'No one wants me anywhere. Why bother?' He said it like someone reading out the weather. I don't know everything going on in his head. But I know one group said no, once, and he's been acting as if every door in the city is shut.

qa.q: What did the older boy tell Varun after one session?
qa.a: The older boy told him, 'We've got enough players, bro.'

qa.q: What might Varun be feeling when he says 'No one wants me anywhere'?
qa.a: Varun likely feels hurt and embarrassed, and shielding himself from another no feels safer than trying, so one refusal gets treated as the answer everywhere.

qa.q: What could help Varun test the rule 'no one wants me'?
qa.a: Varun could try just one badminton session with the cousin as an experiment, to collect a second answer instead of relying on a sample of one.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the change in Varun?
qa.a: Nitin sees a brother shutting himself away after one small rejection, and seems worried and a little frustrated that one 'no' now rules everything.

grounding: Shows, through an older brother's eyes, a teenager rejected once by a football group who acts as if no one anywhere wants him.

passage:
Friday: The seniors running the school robotics team read out the new members. Baljeet's name wasn't there. At the bus stop she told Kiran, 'That's it. No group will ever take me. Robotics, drama, anything. I'm just not someone people pick.'
Tuesday: Kiran slid a poster across the canteen table: 'Nature club: bird count this Sunday.' Baljeet pushed it back. 'Same thing will happen.' Kiran said, 'Then come and prove it.'
Sunday: At 6 a.m. by the lake, a girl from Class 9 lent Baljeet her binoculars, and the teacher asked Baljeet to keep the tally sheet. By nine they had counted forty-two birds. On the way home Baljeet said quietly, 'Okay. Robotics said no. That's one.'

qa.q: How many birds had they counted by nine?
qa.a: By nine they had counted forty-two birds.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet push the nature club poster back on Tuesday?
qa.a: Baljeet felt hurt and discouraged, sure the robotics rejection would repeat anywhere, so pushing the poster away protected her from another no.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did it show?
qa.a: Going to the bird count gave Baljeet a second sample: she was welcomed and trusted with the tally, which showed that one no was only one.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been hoping for by saying 'Then come and prove it'?
qa.a: Kiran likely hoped a real experience would do what arguing couldn't, and trusted that Baljeet would be welcomed somewhere new.

grounding: Shows a teenager refused by the robotics team who decides no group will ever take her, until one new group welcomes her.

passage:
Gautam, you haven't gone out since those boys said the band was full. Come here. Let your Jaya Atya tell you something.

At fourteen, I asked to join the girls who did Rangoli for the school's Diwali competition. They were the popular group. The leader looked at me and said, "We're already enough." Someone giggled.

That night I decided: nobody will ever want me. Not at school, not in college, not anywhere. One group said no, and I made it the whole world's answer.

For a month I ate lunch alone and said no to everything. Then our science teacher made me join the astronomy club because they needed a note-taker. Eight people. They argued about Saturn and fed me their mother's chakli. By Holi they were my people.

One group, Gautam. One. The world is much bigger than one group of Rangoli girls.

qa.q: Which club did the science teacher make Jaya join?
qa.a: The astronomy club.

qa.q: Why did one refusal feel to young Jaya like "nobody will ever want me"?
qa.a: The giggle and the rejection hurt so much that Jaya treated that one group's answer as if the whole world had said no. The pain made a single sample feel like everyone.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Jaya, and what does it suggest for Gautam?
qa.a: Being pushed into the astronomy club, where eight people welcomed her. It suggests Gautam should try another group rather than treating the band's no as final.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel hearing Atya's story?
qa.a: Gautam might feel understood and a bit less stuck, knowing Atya felt the same. The chakli and Saturn details may make trying again feel possible.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, at fourteen, one group's refusal made her decide nobody would ever accept her, until another group welcomed her.

passage:
Chaitanya's family had moved to Siliguri in the middle of the school year, after his father's transfer. He knew nobody, and the family's phone had no data left till the first of the month, so he couldn't even message old friends.

On his third day, he gathered his courage and went up to the boys who played football at lunch. "Can I play?"

Lalit, who seemed to run the group, glanced at him. "Teams are fixed, sorry." And they turned back to the game.

Chaitanya walked back to the classroom with his tiffin unopened. That's it, he thought. Nobody here will ever want me. Nobody anywhere will. I'm just someone people don't take.

For the rest of the week he sat on the classroom step at lunch. Two girls from his row asked if he wanted to join their quiz practice. He shook his head without looking up. What was the point?

qa.q: What did Lalit say when Chaitanya asked to play?
qa.a: "Teams are fixed, sorry."

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya decide nobody anywhere will ever want him after one refusal?
qa.a: He is new, lonely and can't reach old friends, so one no feels like a verdict on him everywhere. The hurt makes a sample of one seem like the whole world.

qa.q: What turning point did Chaitanya miss, and what could he do next?
qa.a: He shook his head when the two girls invited him to quiz practice, which was a real welcome. Next time he could say yes, even just to watch, and test whether everyone really says no.

qa.q: How might the two girls feel when Chaitanya shakes his head without looking up?
qa.a: They might feel brushed off and think he isn't interested in them. They may not ask again, which would make his belief seem truer than it is.

grounding: A new boy refused by one group at school decides nobody will ever accept him, and even turns down a real invitation.
